title: Africa’s green industrial future: the “learning economy” as a prerequisite
body:
Much of the debate on Africa’s green industrialization (GI) focuses on technology, investment, and skills. While these matter, what truly underpins a successful industrialization is a “LEARNING ECONOMY”

A learning economy is one where firms, workers, and institutions continuously experiment, adapt, and upgrade capabilities.

Economic history shows that industrialization is driven not only by investment or resources, but by how effectively societies generate, apply, and diffuse knowledge over time.

The industrial rise of economies such as South Korea, Japan, and Taiwan, were as a result of a deliberately created economic system that learned rapidly and continuously. Notably, workers learnt through experience and problem-solving on the shop floor. Firms learnt through production, experimentation, and competition. Institutions learnt through policy experimentation, coordination, and institutional upgrading.

This continuous interaction between firms, workers, and institutions created a system where knowledge accumulates and spreads across sectors. China is replicating this same model, using it to drive global leadership in several GREEN TECHNOLOGIES.

This insight is particularly important to Africa’s green industrial future.

GI, in its full spectrum, is evolving at extraordinary speed. Technologies are improving, costs are falling, and production methods are constantly changing. In such a world, static capabilities quickly become obsolete. Countries must thus constantly upgrade.

For Africa, this means GI cannot be reduced to building renewable infrastructure or exporting critical minerals. It requires building learning systems where firms experiment, workers accumulate practical knowledge, and institutions support continuous upgrading.

Across successful industrializing economies, 5 learning mechanisms proved particularly powerful:

- Learning-by-doing: Firms and workers build capabilities through production itself.
- Learning-by-using: Technologies are adapted to local conditions, often generating new innovations.
- Learning-by-interacting: Firms collaborate with suppliers, universities, and research institutes, accelerating knowledge diffusion.
- Learning-by-trading: Exposure to global markets through export and/or import pushes firms to upgrade quality, productivity, and technology.
- Adaptive institutions: Governments constantly adjust policies, refine incentives, and respond to new technological and market realities.

**Bottom line:** For Africa to lead in the GI race, it calls for policy shifts that integrates and localizes these learning mechanisms.

This is best summarized this way: i) a shift from human capital strategies to industrial learning strategies; and ii) developing adaptive industrial institutions that experiment, learn from policy outcomes, and adjust strategies as technologies and markets change.
